chapter.label: ch:character-creation

p.emph: a character in Malleus Deum should, hopefully, be relatively straightforward:

olist.li: First choose an archetype for your character, then
Follow the step by step instructions for character creation in that archetype's handbook.

chapter.p: In the rest of the chapter we explain what all the terms and fields on the character sheet mean.

section.p:
Character
Each Player Character has a list of statistics that describe what that character can do and how well they can do it, as follows:

list.li: Five point pools: Stamina, Health, Magic, Mettle, and Luck.
Six Primary Abilities: Strength, Endurance, Agility, Speed, Perception and Will.
Four or more Defensive Abilities, including: Armour, Dodge, Block and Parry.

subsection.p:
Archetype
Each character has an archetype which describes their race, profession, and the set of abilities available to them, for example a character might choose to be a Red Mage or a Halfling Rover.
subsection.design: Archetypes are indivisible because it makes them more modular and allows us to balance one archetype without effecting existing archetypes.

subsection.p:
Level
A character's level represents the characters competence and experience. The character's level usually starts at one, and increases when the GM decides that it is appropriate. As a rule of thumb, characters should gain levels at the end of a story arc or when the players have accomplished something noteworthy in the game.

sec:point-pool
Point Pool Check
Check Point Pool
Point pools represent some finite resource that will run out if overused, for PCs these are Stamina, Health, Magic, Mettle and Luck, but monsters, magic items, and other things can have point pools as well.

Point pools represent some finite resource that the player has to manage during the game, which will run out if overused. When any of the pools is reduced to zero the pool is said to be Exhausted and certain effects are applied as described in the Exhaustion Table. Point pools have a minimum value of zero.

The number of points in a character's point pools are defined by their archetype, level and abilities. For character point pools like Luck, Magic and Mettle the point pools will have a rest rate which allows the player to regain points for each point pool over time when they rest or through the use of other special abilities.
Some point pools can never have their points restored, some magical items. While other point pools can regain their points in a variety of different ways, specified on a case by case basis.

indexentry.indexdefn: When a point pool is reduced to zero that pool is said to be exhausted. This triggers special events in the Exhaustion Table. Any check that requires points to be paid from this pool automatically fail (with the exception of Stamina).

subsubsection.p:
A characters physical well-being is represented by a combination of their Stamina and Health point pools, collectively called their Hit Points
Hit Points .

description.p: Stamina is the characters freshness, their energy, their vigour, and their ability to shrug off minor wounds, bruising, scratches, glancing blows, near misses and the like. Damage to stamina leaves the character breathless, a little stunned, bruised and battered but not physically too badly hurt. As the character's Stamina decreases their ability to avoid serious damage from attackers decreases and the danger of getting really physically hurt increases. Stamina is recovered quickly.

represents the characters brawn, their physical capacity to take damage. Damage to health takes the form of lacerations, deep bruising, sprained joints. Wounds that take time to heal, so it takes time to restore health. The character gains Health back slowly, at their Rest Rate when they Sleep.

subsubsection.p: Characters can take damage to either of these stats as the result of an in-game event. For example, when a character takes damage during combat they will usually take it from their Stamina first and then their Health. Other damage, such as falling damage, applies directly to Health irrespective of the current Stamina.

playexample.p: Dourli, our amiable dwarven friend has somehow managed to find himself in a brawl with some of the towns thugs. Dourli is stabbed by one of the thugs for 4 damage. He only has 3 Stamina remaining so his Stamina is reduced to 0, and his Health is then also reduced by 1. Since Dourli's Stamina is reduced to zero he applies any effects from the Exhaustion Table, he gains the Bloodied keyword, and has to make a Will Check. He fails his Will Check and gains the Checked Condition.

subsubsection.p: A character with zero Stamina gains the Bloodied condition. A character with zero Health gains the Near-Death condition, see pagesec:conditions for more information on conditions. Characters who are Near-Death are effectively too hurt and too weak to defend themselves or do too much and are in danger of dying, see Sectionsec:death on pagesec:death of the GMG. Hit points may be regained in a number of ways, see Sectionsec:healing on pagesec:healing for information on Healing.
The other point pools are as follows:

description.p: Casting magic uses a points from the Magic Point Pool. Casting spells has many special rules, and is described in Sectionch:magic on pagech:magic.
Not all characters are able to cast spells, but all characters have a magic pool. This pool represents their animus, their spark of life, and can be use to resist spells.
This pool measures the characters morale and their current confidence in their situation.

Luck Pool
Characters have a Luck Pool that represents the players manifest destiny, their fate.

subsection.p:
Ability Rank
Rank - Ability
Abilities represent the characters talent, skill, or proficiency in a particular area. Each Ability has a Rank. The higher the ability rank the easier it is for the character to succeed making checks against that ability. Ability ranks are written after the ability. So, for example, we might say that Dourli has Axe Cleave 3, which means that he has Axe Cleave at rank 3.

Characters can have abilities with a Specialization. In this case the specialization will follow the ability name and be written in square brackets, History[Westreich] 2. The template indicates that the knowledge is narrower than the ability name alone suggests. The GM can choose whatever template values they like for templated abilities though some abilities suggest a number of options.

Abilities have numerical ranks. The higher the ability rank the better the character is at that ability and the easier it is for the character to succeed at those ability checks. Ability ranks are written after the ability. So, for example, we might say that Dourli has Axe Cleave 3, which means that he has Axe Cleave at rank 3.

Some abilities have an untrained rank, often 0, -3 or -6. If an ability has an untrained rank then it can be used without training by any character. All characters automatically have all untrained abilities at the untrained rank.

Some abilities have a list of Stages representing some part of the characters current state poisoning or diseases. As the game progresses and characters make or fail checks the stage of the ability may change.

subsubsection.p: All characters share a set of Primary Abilities that describe the characters physical capabilities. These provide a bonus to certain checks and may be prerequisites for other abilities. In Malleus Deum primary abilities are treated like all other abilities, see Sectionsec:primary_abilities on pagesec:primary_abilities.

descriptions.description: insight and ability to notice things

playexample.p: Dourli, our amiable dwarven friend has somehow managed to find himself in a brawl with some of the towns thugs. Dourli is stabbed by one of the thugs for 4 damage. He only has 3 Stamina remaining so his Stamina is reduced to 0, his Health is reduced by 1, he gains the Bloodied keyword, and has to make a Will Check. He fails his Will Check and gains the Checked Condition.

subsubsection.p: Defensive abilities represent how difficult a character is to hit. When an NPC tries to hit a PC in combat the player makes a defensive ability check against the difficulty of the NPC's attack. There are a number of defensive abilities but the three most common are Armour on pageability:armour, Dodge on pageability:dodge, and Block on pageability:block. Some weapon classes also allow the user to parry blows with those weapons, see Staff Parry on pageability:staff.parry, and Sword Parry on pageability:sword.parry. We use the term Defence Check to refer to these ability checks irrespective of the underlying defensive ability the player chooses to make the check.

Common abilities are a set of abilties that are shared by all characters and used frequently. These include abilities like Lore, Brawl and Swim. Every character can attempt these abilities but some archetypes have a higher possibility of success.

All characters have the same set of Primary, Defence and Common abilities. In addition, each character has a range of Specialized Abilities which represent more uncommon or esoteric skills that most other characters do not have, Mighty Blow, Alchemy, Pick Locks, and Phantasmal Leech.

A character's initial abilities are determined by their archetype. The characters archetype assigns a number of abilities for the player to choose from. Abilities have a rank, and might also have one or more specializations. These complications are described further in Chapterch:abilities on pagech:abilities.

Aspects are a special type of ability that describes some facet of the characters personality, relationships, philosophy or oaths : Silent Outcast, Naive Appeaser, Dipsomaniac. Aspects tie those descriptions to game mechanics and allow checks to be made against them, and so have real consequences within the game. Mechanically, Aspects are just another type of Ability, and are defined in detail in Chapterch:aspects on pagech:aspects.

subsection.p: Optionally, players may create a background or backstory for their character. At least some of the players background should be fleshed out at character creation time. The background helps to tie characters to one another and to give them a purpose and a feeling for how they fit in the world. This should be done collaboratively with the GM and possibly with the other players as well to ensure compatibility with the milieu and other character backgrounds.
The player might want to include any supplementary statistics: Height, Weight, Age, Hair Colour and so on.

section.p: At some point in the game the GM will notify the characters that they have leveled up. The archetype document describes the changes available to the character for their new level.
Changes are of the following types.

descriptions.description: The player should modify the level for their character on the character sheet.
The player increases the amount of the relevant hit points on their character sheet.

description.p: The character may gain a completely new ability. The character must be able to learn the ability, and the character must have already gained any prerequisite abilities. Abilities are divided using keywords into a number of categories. For example, the Axe Strike ability has keywords: Weapon, Heavy, Martial, Axe. This means that if the character gains a martial ability when they go up a level they may take the Axe Strike 1 ability or any of the other ability with the keyword martial of the given rank, Sword Strike 1. If the character gains an Axe ability they may only choose from the abilities with the axe keyword. In order to take an ability the abilities prerequisites must be met.

Ability Promotions
Promoting an Ability
An Ability Promotion allows the character to increase the rank of an already mastered ability by one.

Ability Specialization

An ability promotion allows the character to increase the rank of an already mastered ability by one.
